column6: Ich kaufe das Brot beim Bäcker.
column7: I buy the bread at the baker's.
column8: Germany has over 3,000 officially recognized types of bread, the greatest variety in the world.

column7: I drink a glass of water.
column8: In German restaurants tap water is almost never served: you order it 'still' (flat) or 'mit Kohlensäure' (sparkling).
German houses often have a 'Keller' (cellar) used as storage or a hobby room, less common in southern Europe.

column6: Wir gehen heute in den Park.
column7: We're going to the park today.
column8: The verb 'gehen' forms dozens of expressions: 'es geht mir gut' (I'm well) literally means 'it goes well for me'.

column6: Der Apfel ist rot und süß.
column7: The apple is red and sweet.
column8: The Streuobstwiese, a traditional orchard meadow, is a protected landscape in Germany where dozens of old apple varieties still grow.

column6: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab.
column7: The train departs at eight o'clock.
column8: Germany's rail network is run by Deutsche Bahn, and punctuality matters so much that delays regularly make the national news.
Germans distinguish 'Arbeit' (paid labor) from 'Beruf' (vocation/calling): the idea that a job should also be a calling runs deep in German work culture.

column7: I don't have any money on me.
column8: 'Kein' negates nouns while 'nicht' negates verbs and adjectives — a distinction that trips up speakers of Romance languages.

column6: Am Samstag gehe ich auf den Markt.
column7: On Saturday I go to the market.
column8: Wochenmärkte (weekly markets) are a civic institution in Germany: almost every town has one, and shopping there is seen as eco-friendly and community-minded.

column7: I'm going to the doctor tomorrow.
column8: In Germany the Hausarzt (family doctor) acts as a gatekeeper: you usually need a referral to see a specialist.
The casual greeting 'Tag!' is short for 'Guten Tag' and is heard everywhere in shops and on the street.

column7: In the morning I drink coffee.
column8: In Germany coffee is mainly drunk in the morning and in the afternoon with a slice of cake — the ritual is called 'Kaffee und Kuchen'.
In German 'Freund' implies a deep bond: mere acquaintances are called 'Bekannte'. Calling someone a 'Freund' carries more weight than in English.
Many German cities have a pedestrian 'Altstadt' (old town) carefully rebuilt after the war.

column6: Wir essen um zwölf Uhr zu Mittag.
column7: We eat lunch at twelve o'clock.
column8: In many German companies and schools, the main hot meal is at midday, not in the evening.

column6: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
column7: The book is lying on the table.
column8: The Frankfurt Book Fair is the world's largest publishing event and has run continuously since 1949.
In Germany people still often pay in cash: many small shops don't accept cards.

column6: Mein Zimmer ist klein, aber hell.
column7: My room is small but bright.
column8: In German property listings, the room count ('3-Zimmer-Wohnung') doesn't include the kitchen or bathroom.
'Woher kommst du?' is one of the first questions in a German conversation, and people expect the city or region, not just the country.
Countless German streets are named after poets and philosophers: Goethe, Schiller, and Kant each have a street in almost every town.

column7: On the weekend I sleep in.
column8: In Germany it's common to use two single duvets on a double bed instead of one shared blanket.
German 'Kaffee' usually means filtered drip coffee — for an Italian-style espresso you have to ask for it specifically.

column7: The child is playing in the garden.
column8: 'Kindergarten' is a German invention from 1840: the word has entered dozens of languages unchanged.
The verb changes vowel in the second and third person: 'du sprichst', 'er spricht' — the same pattern as 'essen' and 'geben'.
In Germany, talking openly about salaries is considered rather impolite — much more so than in many other countries.
A traditional Bavarian 'Biergarten' only opens when the weather allows it: the weather is an everyday conversation topic.

column6: Ich fahre mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
column7: I go to work by bus.
column8: German distinguishes 'gehen' (on foot) from 'fahren' (by vehicle): you can't 'gehen' to Berlin by train.
Sunday in Germany is traditionally reserved for family: shops are closed, and there's the afternoon 'Sonntagsspaziergang' (Sunday walk).
In German, 'lernen' means to learn or study for school; 'studieren' is used only for university studies.

column6: Der Bahnhof ist nicht weit von hier.
column7: The train station isn't far from here.
column8: The expression 'Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof' ('I only understand station') means 'I don't understand a thing'.
German cardinal numbers are often written as a single word even for very high figures: 'einhundertdreiundzwanzig' is all one word.
In handwritten German, 'zwei' gets a dash through its leg so it isn't confused with 'sieben' (seven) or a one.
'Aller guten Dinge sind drei' ('all good things come in threes') is the German way of saying 'third time's the charm'.
German uses 'zu viert' to say 'the four of us', a compact construction with no preposition needed.
'Fünf gerade sein lassen' ('let five be even') means to turn a blind eye to something.

column6: Der Kurs beginnt um sechs Uhr.
column7: The course starts at six o'clock.
column8: Formal German uses the 24-hour clock even in everyday speech more often than English typically does.
'Siebenmal klug' ('seven times clever') describes a know-it-all who always has to be right.
'Acht geben' means 'to pay attention' — a very common expression with no historical link to the number eight.
In many German towns shops open later than in Italy, often not before nine.
'Zehn' underlies all German numerals from 'elf' (eleven) upward, formed by addition or multiplication.

column6: Am Montag beginnt die Arbeit wieder.
column8: In German, the days of the week are always masculine and, like all nouns, are capitalized.
'Dienstag' comes from 'Ding', the old Germanic assembly, not from the god Mars as in Romance languages.

column6: Mittwoch ist die Mitte der Woche.
column7: Wednesday is the middle of the week.
column8: 'Mittwoch' literally means 'mid-week' — the only German weekday named for its position rather than for a god.
'Donnerstag' is the day of Thor/Donar, the god of thunder — the same root as the English 'Thursday'.
'Freitag' is named after the goddess Frigg — the most eagerly awaited day of the German working week.
Southern Germany says 'Samstag'; the north more often says 'Sonnabend' — one of the best-known regional differences.

column7: On Sundays the shops are closed.
column8: Sunday in Germany is protected by law: almost all shops stay closed the entire day.
'Mutter' is one of the most stable Indo-European words: nearly identical across dozens of languages.
'Vatertag', German Father's Day, falls on Ascension Day and is traditionally a men's outing with beer and handcarts.
The plural 'Brüder' takes an umlaut — a typical pattern for one-syllable German masculine nouns.
'Geschwister' is the collective word for 'siblings' as a group, with no gender distinction.
In everyday speech almost everyone says 'Oma' instead of the full form 'Großmutter'.
In everyday speech people usually say 'Opa'; 'Großvater' is the neutral or more formal form.
In German 'keine Milch' negates the noun directly, while English negates the verb with 'don't'.
Germany produces over 600 types of cheese — less famous abroad than French or Italian cheeses, but very varied.

column6: Zum Frühstück esse ich ein Ei.
column7: For breakfast I eat an egg.
column8: 'Ei' is one of the shortest German nouns; the plural 'Eier' adds a whole extra syllable.
'Kein Fleisch essen' is the standard way to say you're vegetarian, much more common than saying 'Vegetarier sein'.

column6: Am Freitag gibt es oft Fisch.
column8: The Catholic tradition of fish on Fridays survives in German cafeteria menus even outside a religious context.
'Gemüse' is a singular collective noun: there's no common plural, unlike English 'vegetables'.
Like 'Gemüse', 'Obst' is always a singular collective noun: you can't say 'three fruits', you need 'drei Obstsorten' (three kinds of fruit).
In German cafeterias, soup is often the standard starter, served at lunch nearly every day.
'Salz' is neuter: 'das Salz'. The fixed pair is 'Salz und Pfeffer', always in this order.
'Zucker' is almost always uncountable in German, just like in English: you say 'etwas Zucker' (some sugar), not 'ein Zucker'.
At a German bar, you can order beer with the plain unchanged plural 'zwei Bier' — no suffix needed.

column6: Der Wein kommt aus der Region.
column7: The wine comes from the region.
column8: Germany's most famous wine regions, like the Moselle, mostly produce white wines, unlike Italy.

column6: Ich hätte gern eine Tasse Tee.
column7: I'd like a cup of tea.
column8: 'Ich hätte gern' is the standard polite way to order, more courteous than the plain 'ich will' (I want).
'Einen Teller voll haben' ('to have a full plate') is also used figuratively to mean having too much to do.
'Auf Messers Schneide stehen' ('to stand on a knife's edge') means being in a very delicate situation.
The word 'Gabel' shares a root with 'gabeln' (to fork/branch off) — the shape echoes its prongs.

column6: Nimm einen Löffel für die Suppe.
column7: Take a spoon for the soup.
column8: 'Über den Löffel balbieren' ('to shave with a spoon') is an old saying meaning 'to trick someone'.
'Fenster' comes from the Latin 'fenestra', one of the few old Romance loanwords still in everyday German.
'Tür' is feminine: 'die Tür'. 'Die Tür aufmachen/zumachen' = to open/close the door. 'Tor' is a gate or a football goal.
'Reinen Tisch machen' ('to make a clean table') means to clear the air once and for all.
The plural 'Stühle' takes an umlaut, like many common one-syllable masculine nouns.
'Ins Bett gehen' uses the accusative because it describes movement toward a place, not a static position.

column7: The clothes are in the wardrobe.
column8: 'Schrank' can mean any closed piece of furniture: wardrobe, cabinet, or even the regional word for fridge, 'Kühlschrank'.
'Anmachen' for lights is casual and very common; the more formal word would be 'einschalten'.
'In den Spiegel schauen' takes the accusative because the gaze is directed toward the mirror, a kind of mental movement.

column6: Im Sommer sitzen wir im Garten.
column7: In summer we sit in the garden.
column8: Many Germans living in cities rent a small 'Schrebergarten', an allotment garden outside the home — a tradition over a century old.

column6: Ich kaufe Blumen für meine Mutter.
column7: I'm buying flowers for my mother.
column8: Giving an even number of flowers is considered bad taste in Germany — an odd number is always preferred.

column6: Der Baum vor unserem Haus ist sehr alt.
column7: The tree in front of our house is very old.
column8: The 'Tannenbaum' (fir tree) is at the heart of German Christmas traditions, which also gave the famous carol its name.
In Germany dogs are allowed in many restaurants, shops, and on public transport, often with a discounted ticket.

column6: Die Katze schläft den ganzen Tag.
column8: 'Die Katze im Sack kaufen' ('to buy the cat in the sack') matches the English 'to buy a pig in a poke' — buying blind.

column7: A bird is singing in the tree.
column8: 'Einen Vogel haben' ('to have a bird') means being a bit crazy — a very common, casual expression.

column6: Sie reitet jeden Samstag ein Pferd.
column7: She rides a horse every Saturday.
column8: 'Das Pferd von hinten aufzäumen' ('to saddle the horse from behind') means tackling a problem the wrong way round.
German adjectives take an ending that changes with case, gender, and article: 'rotes' here agrees with the neuter noun 'Kleid'.
In colloquial German, 'blau sein' ('to be blue') also means 'to be drunk', not just to describe a color.
Germany's ecologist party is simply called 'Die Grünen' (The Greens), one of the most influential in Europe.
'Das ist nicht das Gelbe vom Ei' ('that's not the yolk of the egg') means something isn't all that great.
'Schwarzarbeit' (black work) is a widely used German term for undeclared, off-the-books labor.
'Weiß' (white) and the verb form 'ich weiß' (I know, from 'wissen') look identical but are unrelated — a trap for learners.
In the comparative, 'groß' becomes irregular: 'größer, am größten', gaining an umlaut.

column6: Die Wohnung ist klein, aber gemütlich.
column7: The apartment is small but cosy.
column8: 'Klein aber fein' ('small but fine') is a very positive way to describe something compact and well made.
In the comparative, 'alt' becomes 'älter': the umlaut appears regularly in many one-syllable German adjectives.
Unlike 'alt', 'neu' doesn't take an umlaut in the comparative: 'neuer, am neuesten'.
'Gut' is irregular in the comparative: 'besser, am besten', just like English 'good, better, best'.
'Mir geht es schlecht' uses the dative 'mir': grammatically, your mood 'happens to you' in German rather than being something you control.
In German, many adjectives also work as adverbs without changing form, unlike English which often adds '-ly'.
Asking someone to speak 'langsam' is one of the first useful phrases every beginner learns in German.
'Ein heißes Eisen' ('a hot iron') refers to a delicate topic that needs careful handling.

column6: Im Winter ist es sehr kalt.
column8: 'Kalte Füße bekommen' ('to get cold feet') means losing your nerve at the last moment, just like the English idiom.
'Müde' describes both physical tiredness and running out of patience: 'ich bin es müde' means 'I'm sick of it'.
In German you can say either 'hungrig sein' or 'Hunger haben' — both are common in everyday speech.

column6: Nach dem Sport bin ich durstig.
column8: Just like 'hungrig', there's also 'Durst haben' — the two constructions are interchangeable in everyday language.
'Ein Auge zudrücken' ('to press one eye shut') means to forgive or deliberately overlook a small mistake.
'Hand' appears in dozens of German expressions: 'zur Hand haben' means to have something within reach.
Pain in German is often expressed with the indirect dative: the full form is 'mein Kopf tut mir weh' (my head hurts me).

column6: Ich gehe zu Fuß zur Arbeit.
column8: 'Zu Fuß gehen' is a fixed expression with no article: saying 'mit dem Fuß' instead would completely change the meaning.
'Herz' is one of the few neuter nouns with an irregular declension in the genitive and dative: 'des Herzens', 'dem Herzen'.
In Germany, a doctor's note ('Krankschreibung') is almost always required starting from the third day of absence.
'Gesund' is also the root of 'Gesundheit', used as a well-wish after someone sneezes.
'Woche' is feminine: 'die Woche', plural 'Wochen'. 'Nächste Woche' is used without a preposition.
'Monat' shares a root with 'Mond' (moon): the German month, as in many languages, comes from the lunar cycle.

column6: Ich lerne seit einem Jahr Deutsch.
column7: I've been learning German for a year.
column8: 'Seit einem Jahr' uses the dative after 'seit' together with the present tense, not the past as in 'I have studied'.
'Heute' often takes first position in the sentence, pushing the verb into second position under the V2 rule.

column7: Tomorrow I have the day off.
column8: Lowercase 'morgen' is the adverb 'tomorrow'; capitalized 'Morgen' is the noun 'morning' — the capital letter changes everything.

column7: Yesterday I was at the cinema.
column8: With 'gestern', spoken German almost always uses the Perfekt ('war', 'bin gegangen'), not the simple past used in writing.
Like 'heute', 'jetzt' often pushes the verb into second position when placed at the start of the sentence.
'Besser spät als nie' ('better late than never') is a direct match with English, a rare case of an exact calque.
'Früh' is the root of 'Frühstück' (breakfast), literally the 'early piece' of the meal.
'Keine Zeit haben' with 'kein' negates the noun 'Zeit' directly, unlike English which negates the verb 'have'.
'Uhr' is used both for the clock itself and to state the exact time, just like English 'o'clock'.

column6: Die Kinder gehen in die Schule.
column8: 'In die Schule gehen' uses the accusative because it describes movement toward a specific place.
The feminine form is 'Lehrerin': almost every German profession noun has a '-in' ending for the feminine.
'Schüler' is used for compulsory schooling; once at university you become a 'Student', no longer a 'Schüler'.
'Mit dem Auto fahren' uses the dative after 'mit' — one of the most frequent dative prepositions in everyday German.
In many German cities, the bicycle is the main everyday mode of transport, with bike lanes everywhere.
'Bus' is a shortened loanword from the Latin 'omnibus' (for everyone), which passed through French on its way into German.
'Flugzeug' is a transparent compound: 'Flug' (flight) + 'Zeug' (tool/thing) — literally a 'flying tool'.

column7: The ship is sailing to Norway.
column8: Hamburg has one of the largest ports in Europe, and its history is deeply tied to shipping.

column6: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Bahnhof.
column7: We're taking a taxi to the station.
column8: In many German cities, taxis look almost identical — often cream-colored Mercedes — and run on fixed municipal fares.
German low-cost airlines check carry-on baggage weight with great strictness.
'Pass' is short for 'Reisepass'. The identity card is the 'Personalausweis'; 'Ausweis' means an ID document in general.

column6: Ich kaufe eine Karte für den Zug.
column7: I'm buying a ticket for the train.
column8: 'Karte' is a very versatile word: it means ticket, credit card, postcard, or map depending on context.

column6: Das Geschäft schließt um achtzehn Uhr.
column7: The shop closes at eighteen o'clock.
column8: 'Geschäft' means both the physical shop and a business deal in the abstract sense — two meanings in one word.
'Preis' means both 'price' and 'prize': a 'Nobelpreis' is a prize, not a price to pay.
'Billig' often carries a slightly negative connotation of poor quality; 'günstig' (good value) sounds more neutral and positive.
In big German cities like Munich or Berlin, rents have risen enormously over the last decade.
The standard German rental contract is open-ended: fixed-term leases are the exception, not the rule.
'Nummer' refers to identifying numbers (phone, house); for pure mathematics, 'Zahl' is used instead.

column6: Kannst du mir deine Adresse geben?
column7: Can you give me your address?
column8: In German, an address is written with street and house number before the postal code and city — a different order from English.
In German 'E-Mail' is feminine, even though English has no grammatical gender: loanwords often get their gender by analogy with a similar German word ('die Post').
'Telefon' is neuter, and 'Handy' (mobile phone, an invented German word that doesn't exist with this meaning in English) is neuter too.
'Handy' looks like an English word but is a false loan: in British or American English it isn't used with this meaning at all.
In German, 'Computer' is stressed on the second syllable, differently from English.
In many rural parts of Germany, internet connections are surprisingly slower than in other major European economies.
Germany has a very long classical music tradition: Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms were all German.
Foreign films in Germany are almost always dubbed into German, rather than subtitled as in other European countries.

column6: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
column7: The picture is hanging on the wall.
column8: 'Ein Bild von einem Menschen' ('a picture of a person') is an idiom for saying someone is very good-looking.
'Farbe bekennen' ('to confess color') means to state your opinion clearly — an expression that comes from card games.

column7: I need a sheet of paper.
column8: Germany is among the European countries with the highest per-capita paper consumption, despite a strong recycling culture.

column6: Hast du einen Stift für mich?
column7: Do you have a pen for me?
column8: 'Stift' is a generic term for writing implements; to be precise, you say 'Kugelschreiber' (ballpoint pen) or 'Bleistift' (pencil).

column6: Ich habe meinen Schlüssel in der Tasche.
column7: I have my key in my pocket.
column8: 'Tasche' means both 'bag' and 'clothing pocket' — context makes clear which one is meant.
'Der Schlüssel zum Erfolg' ('the key to success') is a figurative expression identical in German and English.
'Regenschirm' is a transparent compound: 'Regen' (rain) + 'Schirm' (screen/shield).

column6: Im Sommer trage ich eine Sonnenbrille.
column8: 'Brille' is always singular in German for a single pair of glasses, whereas English uses the plural 'glasses'.
'Das Hemd ist mir näher als der Rock' ('the shirt is closer to me than the skirt') is the German way of saying charity begins at home.
'Hose' is always singular in German, while English 'trousers' is plural — a classic trap for learners.
'Wo drückt der Schuh?' ('where does the shoe pinch?') figuratively means 'what's the problem?'

column6: Zieh deine Jacke an, es ist kalt.
column7: Put your jacket on, it's cold.
column8: 'Anziehen' is separable: in the present tense it becomes 'ich ziehe an', with the prefix 'an-' at the end of the sentence.

column6: Im Winter trage ich eine Mütze.
column7: In winter I wear a beanie.
column8: 'Mütze' refers to soft, brimless hats; for a stiff hat with a visor, German instead uses 'Hut' or 'Kappe'.

column6: Im Sommer fahren wir ans Meer.
column7: In summer we go to the sea.
column8: 'Sommerferien' (summer holidays) vary by region in Germany, so not everyone travels at the same time.

column6: Der Winter ist hier sehr kalt.
column8: In many German regions, Christmas markets already open in late November and are a central part of winter.
'Frühling' shares a root with 'früh' (early): the season that arrives 'early' after winter.

column6: Im Herbst werden die Blätter bunt.
column7: In autumn the leaves turn colorful.
column8: In many parts of Germany, autumn is fondly called 'goldener Herbst' (golden autumn) for the color of the foliage.
'Sonne' (sun) is feminine in German, while 'Mond' (moon) is masculine — the opposite of many Romance languages.
'Aufhören' is separable: 'hört auf' in the present tense, with the prefix detached at the end of the main clause.
'Schnee von gestern' ('yesterday's snow') is the German equivalent of 'water under the bridge' — something no longer relevant.
Northern Germany, on the North Sea, is among Europe's windiest regions and home to many wind farms.
'Auf den Berg' uses the accusative because it describes movement toward the summit, not a fixed position.

column6: Der Rhein ist ein großer Fluss.
column7: The Rhine is a big river.
column8: The Rhine flows through Germany from south to north and is historically the country's most important trade route.
Careful: 'der See' (masculine) is the lake, while 'die See' (feminine) means 'the sea' in northern German usage.

column6: Im Urlaub fahren wir ans Meer.
column7: On vacation we go to the sea.
column8: 'Ans Meer fahren' uses the contraction 'an das' → 'ans', very common with prepositions and neuter articles.

column7: We're going for a walk in the forest.
column8: The forest holds deep cultural meaning in Germany, from the Brothers Grimm fairy tales to the modern environmental movement.

column6: Ein gelbes Blatt fällt vom Baum.
column7: A yellow leaf falls from the tree.
column8: 'Blatt' means both 'leaf' and 'sheet of paper' — the same image of something thin and flat.

column7: The fire is burning in the fireplace.
column8: 'Feuer und Flamme sein' ('to be fire and flame') means to be really enthusiastic about something.
'Ausmachen' is separable: 'mach aus' in the imperative, with the prefix detached at the end.
In many German schools, learning a musical instrument is part of the curriculum from primary school onward.
In German you say 'Gitarre spielen' with no article before the instrument, unlike English 'play the guitar'.
'Klavier' comes from the French 'clavier', while other Germanic languages prefer 'Piano' — a different loanword.

column7: The children are singing a song.
column8: 'Singen' is a strong irregular verb: 'sang, gesungen', with the vowel change typical of old Germanic verbs.
'Tanzen' is regular: 'tanzte, getanzt', unlike many old Germanic verbs of motion.

column7: The children are playing in the park.
column8: 'Spielen' is used both for playing and for playing an instrument — context tells the two meanings apart.
'Lachen' is regular in the Perfekt: 'haben gelacht', using 'haben' because it doesn't describe motion.
'Weinen' (to cry) and 'Wein' (wine) look similar but aren't etymologically related at all.
'Helfen' takes the dative: 'mir helfen', not the accusative as in a literal 'help me'.

column6: Ich danke dir für die Hilfe.
column7: I thank you for your help.
column8: 'Danken' takes the dative: 'dir danken', where a literal 'thank you' would suggest the accusative.
'Fragen' takes the accusative for the person: 'ich frage dich', unlike 'helfen' and 'danken', which want the dative.
'Antworten' takes the dative of the person being answered: 'mir antworten', not the accusative.
'Verstehen' isn't separable even though 'ver-' looks like a detachable prefix: it belongs to the inseparable-prefix class.
'Wissen' is used for concrete facts; for knowing people or places German uses 'kennen' instead — a distinction English doesn't make.
'Kennen' and 'wissen' both translate as 'to know' in English, but in German they are never interchangeable.
'Denken an' takes the accusative: 'an dich denken' — a fixed structure worth memorizing.
'Glauben' takes the dative when you believe a person ('ich glaube dir') but no special case when you believe a fact.
'Mögen' is an irregular modal verb: 'ich mag, du magst, er mag', with a vowel change from the infinitive.
As a modal, 'wollen' sends the main verb to the infinitive at the end of the sentence: 'ich will gehen'.
'Können' expresses both physical ability and a learned skill: 'ich kann schwimmen' means 'I know how to swim'.
'Müssen' expresses objective necessity; for a moral or social obligation, 'sollen' is often preferred instead.
'Sollen' expresses advice or an outside expectation, different from the practical necessity expressed by 'müssen'.

column7: I have to tidy my room.
column8: 'Aufräumen' is separable: in the present tense 'räume auf', with the prefix detached at the end of the main clause.

column6: Kannst du bitte den Tisch decken?
column7: Can you please set the table?
column8: 'Den Tisch decken' is a fixed expression: 'decken' alone means 'to cover', not 'to set', in other contexts.

column6: Ich mache jeden Morgen mein Bett.
column7: I make my bed every morning.
column8: 'Machen' is one of the most versatile German verbs: 'Kaffee machen', 'Hausaufgaben machen', 'Bett machen' — all different meanings.
'Sich die Zähne putzen' uses the reflexive dative 'mir' plus the accusative 'die Zähne' — a double structure typical of German.
'Duschen' is a loanword from the Italian 'doccia' by way of French, only arriving in German in the 19th century.
'Sich anziehen' is reflexive and separable at the same time — two grammatical complexities in a single verb.
A traditional German breakfast includes bread, cheese, and cold cuts — very different from a sweet Italian breakfast.
'Zum Mittagessen' uses the contraction 'zu dem' → 'zum', very common before masculine and neuter nouns.
In many German families, dinner is a cold meal of bread and cold cuts, while the hot meal is eaten at lunch.

column7: Today we're going to the restaurant.
column8: 'Ins Restaurant' uses the contraction 'in das' → 'ins': movement toward a place always takes the accusative.
'Speisekarte' is a compound: 'Speise' (dish) + 'Karte' (card), literally a 'card of dishes'.
'Bestellen' isn't separable even though it starts with 'be-': verbs with this prefix are always inseparable.
'Zahlen' and 'bezahlen' are near-synonyms, but 'zahlen' is more typical in the context of a restaurant bill.
'Elf' and 'zwölf' are the only exceptions in the German number system between ten and twenty: they don't follow the '-zehn' pattern.

column6: Der Tag hat zwölf Stunden Licht.
column7: The day has twelve hours of light.
column8: 'Ein Dutzend' (a dozen) corresponds exactly to 'zwölf' — a unit still used by the baker.
From 'zwanzig' onward, all numbers are built by addition: 'einundzwanzig' is literally 'one-and-twenty'.
German decades from 'dreißig' onward have an irregular ending ('-ßig'), different from the normal '-zig' of 'zwanzig', 'vierzig', etc.

column7: The book has a hundred pages.
column8: 'Hundert' does not change and is written together with units: 'zweihundert', 'dreihundert'.
'Onkel' comes from the French 'oncle': one of many Romance loanwords that entered German through 18th-century aristocratic culture.
Like 'Onkel', 'Tante' is also a French loanword, entering German along with many courtly words in the 18th century.
The pronunciation of 'Cousin' stays very close to the original French, keeping the final nasal sound.

column7: The baby is sleeping right now.
column8: 'Baby' is a direct loanword from English, kept with no spelling changes but assigned neuter gender by convention.
The suffix '-schaft' forms feminine abstract nouns, as in 'Freundschaft' (friendship) or 'Gesellschaft' (society).

column6: Das Postamt ist gleich um die Ecke.
column7: The post office is just around the corner.
column8: In many German towns today, postal counters are often found inside stationery shops or newsstands rather than dedicated buildings.
Careful: 'die Bank' means 'bank', but 'die Bank' also means 'bench' — the same word, a different context.

column7: The pharmacy is on emergency duty today.
column8: German pharmacies are marked by a large stylized red 'A', recognizable in every town.
'Einkaufen' with 'im Supermarkt' describes a habitual action, not a single movement, which is why it takes the dative.

column7: Shall we go to the cinema today?
column8: 'Ins Kino gehen' is a fixed expression that always takes the accusative, for movement toward the place.

column7: She likes going to the theatre.
column8: Publicly subsidized theatre is widespread in Germany: almost every mid-sized city has its own Stadttheater.

column7: The museum is closed on Sundays.
column8: Berlin has a 'Museumsinsel' (museum island), a UNESCO World Heritage site with five major museums on one small island.

column6: Wir machen einen Spaziergang im Park.
column7: We're taking a walk in the park.
column8: 'Einen Spaziergang machen' is the standard way to say 'to go for a walk', more common than the plain verb 'spazieren'.
In Germany the single emergency number is 112, valid across the whole EU for ambulance, fire brigade, and police.
'Polizei' is always a singular collective noun in German, just like in English: there's no plural 'Polizeien'.

column7: The fire brigade is putting out the fire.
column8: 'Feuerwehr' is a compound: 'Feuer' (fire) + 'Wehr' (defense), literally 'defense against fire'.
'Beruf' shares a root with 'berufen' (to call): it historically meant a true calling, not just a job.
In German, after 'sein' (to be), professions are used without an article: 'ich bin Lehrer', not 'ich bin ein Lehrer'.
The masculine form 'Krankenpfleger' is increasingly used as a gender-neutral term in this profession.

column6: Der Koch bereitet das Essen zu.
column7: The cook is preparing the meal.
column8: 'Zubereiten' has a historically mixed prefix, but in modern usage it is always inseparable.

column7: The shop assistant is happy to help me.
column8: 'Verkäufer' comes from the verb 'verkaufen' (to sell) with the agentive suffix '-er', very productive in German.

column7: The secretary organizes all the appointments.
column8: The suffix '-in' makes almost every German profession noun feminine: 'Sekretär' → 'Sekretärin'.
'Chef' comes from French and keeps its original pronunciation with an initial 'sh' sound, not a German 'k'.
'Firma' is one of the rare German nouns ending in '-a' that stays feminine even in its irregular plural, 'Firmen'.
'Im Büro arbeiten' uses the dative because it describes a fixed position, not movement toward a place.
Despite the existing German word 'Besprechung', 'Meeting' is now extremely common in corporate language.
'Pause machen' is a fixed expression: no indefinite article is needed before 'Pause' in this context.

column7: The children will soon have holidays.
column8: 'Ferien' is always plural in German and refers to school holidays; for time off work German uses 'Urlaub' instead.
In Germany, wishing someone a happy birthday early is thought to bring bad luck — people always wait for the exact day.
'Fest' is the root of 'Festival', 'Oktoberfest', and many other words tied to German celebrations.

column6: Wir feiern Weihnachten bei der Familie.
column7: We celebrate Christmas with the family.
column8: 'Weihnachten' is historically both singular and plural in grammar; today it's almost always treated as neuter singular.

column6: An Ostern besuchen wir die Großeltern.
column7: At Easter we visit the grandparents.
column8: 'Ostern' shares a root with 'Osten' (east): some theories trace it to the name of an old Germanic dawn goddess.

column7: On New Year's Eve there are fireworks.
column8: 'Silvester' is named after Pope Sylvester I, whose feast day falls on December 31st in the Catholic calendar.

column7: I am giving my mother flowers.
column8: 'Schenken' takes the dative for the person (meiner Mutter) and the accusative for the gift (Blumen). Perfekt: 'hat geschenkt'.

column7: I wish you a happy birthday.
column8: 'Gratulieren' takes the dative of the person: 'dir gratulieren', another of German's many dative verbs.

column6: Wir laden alle Freunde zur Feier ein.
column7: We're inviting all our friends to the party.
column8: 'Zur Feier' is the contraction of 'zu der Feier': 'zu' always takes the dative.

column7: We're sitting in the living room.
column8: 'Wohnzimmer' is a transparent compound: 'wohnen' (to live) + 'Zimmer' (room) — the room you spend the most time in.
In many German homes the bedrooms are upstairs, while the living room and kitchen stay on the ground floor.
In many German apartments, the toilet is in a separate room ('Toilette') from the bathroom with the shower or tub.

column7: The wine bottles are in the cellar.
column8: Almost every German house has a Keller, used as storage, a wine cellar, or a hobby room — a typical architectural feature.
Red pitched roofs are a distinctive feature of the architecture of many German towns, especially in the south.

column7: We have breakfast on the balcony.
column8: 'Auf dem Balkon' uses the dative because it describes a position, not movement toward the balcony.
'Aufzug' comes from the verb 'aufziehen' (to pull up) — a much more concrete term than the French-derived 'Lift', also used regionally.
'Die Treppe hoch gehen' is a common colloquial structure, an alternative to the more formal 'die Treppe hinaufgehen'.
'Schicken' takes the dative for the person and the accusative for the thing sent: 'dir eine Nachricht schicken'.

column6: Die Ankunft des Zuges ist um zehn Uhr.
column7: The train's arrival is at ten o'clock.
column8: 'Ankunft' is feminine and comes from 'ankommen'. The opposite is 'Abfahrt' (departure).
'Warten auf' takes the accusative: 'auf dich warten', a fixed structure to memorize together with the verb.
'Suchen' always takes a direct accusative object, with no preposition needed, unlike many Romance languages.
'Finden' is also used to express an opinion: 'ich finde das gut' means 'I think that's good'.
'Verlieren' is a strong irregular verb: 'verlor, verloren', with the vowel changing twice.

column7: Can you bring me some water?
column8: 'Bringen' takes the dative of the person and the accusative of the thing brought — a common double-object structure.

column6: Ich nehme den Bus um acht.
column7: I take the bus at eight.
column8: 'Nehmen' is irregular: 'du nimmst, er nimmt', with the e-i vowel change typical of many strong verbs.
'Es gibt' ('there is / there are') is one of the most-used German structures and always takes the accusative, not the nominative.
'Sehen' is irregular in the second and third person: 'du siehst, er sieht', with an e-ie vowel change.

column7: I like listening to the radio.
column8: 'Hören' is regular, unlike 'sehen' — a good example of how German sense verbs don't follow one single pattern.
'Riechen' can describe both perceiving a smell and giving one off: 'ich rieche das' and 'es riecht gut' use the same verb.
'Schmecken' takes the dative when specifying who likes it: 'es schmeckt mir' means 'I like the taste of it'.
'Sich fühlen' is reflexive: the pronoun 'mich' is mandatory and changes according to the person speaking.
'Kleidung' is a collective noun that's always singular, like 'Gemüse' or 'Obst', with no common plural.
'Rock' means 'skirt' in German, not 'rock' the stone or the music genre — a classic false friend for English speakers.
'Kleid' in its plural 'Kleider' also means 'clothes' in general — a collective term for clothing.

column7: I'm looking for a clean sock.
column8: 'Sich auf die Socken machen' ('to put oneself on the socks') is a colloquial expression for 'to get going, hurry up'.

column7: The belt is made of leather.
column8: 'Den Gürtel enger schnallen' ('to tighten the belt') means having to cut back on spending, just like the English idiom.
In Germany the engagement ring is often worn on the left hand, moving to the right after the wedding.
'Tragen' is irregular: 'er trägt', Perfekt 'hat getragen'. It means both 'to wear' and 'to carry'; context tells which.

column6: Ich laufe jeden Morgen im Park.
column7: I run in the park every morning.
column8: In southern German dialects, 'laufen' often simply means 'to walk', while in the north it more specifically means 'to run'.
The Perfekt of 'schwimmen' uses 'sein': 'ich bin geschwommen', because it describes movement with a change of state.

column7: The child is jumping for joy.
column8: 'Springen' uses 'sein' in the Perfekt when it describes movement: 'ich bin gesprungen'.

column6: Die Kinder klettern auf den Baum.
column7: The children are climbing the tree.
column8: 'Klettern' is very popular in Germany as a sport: indoor climbing gyms are common in almost every city.
'Reisen' uses 'sein' in the Perfekt: 'ich bin gereist', because it describes moving from one place to another.
'Ankommen' always uses 'sein' in the Perfekt: 'ich bin angekommen', never 'haben', because it describes a change of position.

column7: The plane takes off on time.
column8: 'Abfliegen' is separable: in the present tense 'fliegt ab', with the prefix detached at the end of the main clause.

column6: Ich muss noch meinen Koffer packen.
column7: I still have to pack my suitcase.
column8: 'Packen' takes a direct accusative object with no preposition: 'den Koffer packen' (to pack the suitcase).
In Germany, carrying a valid ID document at all times is a legal requirement.

column6: Bitte füllen Sie das Formular aus.
column8: 'Ausfüllen' is separable: 'füllen Sie aus' in the formal imperative, with the prefix detached at the end.
'Unterschrift' is a compound: 'unter' (under) + 'Schrift' (writing), literally 'writing under' the document.

column7: The doctor is writing a prescription.
column8: 'Rezept' means both 'medical prescription' and 'cooking recipe' — the German word covers both senses, just like in Italian.
'Fieber haben' needs no article before the noun — a fixed structure common with many symptoms.

column7: I've had a cough for days.
column8: 'Seit Tagen' uses the dative plural after 'seit', paired with the present tense for an action still ongoing.

column7: I'm in a lot of pain.
column8: 'Schmerzen' is almost always used in the plural in German for physical pain, even for a single localized ache.

column6: Nimm diese Tablette gegen die Schmerzen.
column7: Take this pill for the pain.
column8: 'Gegen' always takes the accusative: 'gegen die Schmerzen' (against the pain) — a very common preposition in medical contexts.
In Germany, health insurance has been a legal requirement since 1883 — the first system of its kind in the world.

column6: In der Mittagspause essen wir in der Kantine.
column7: We eat in the canteen during the lunch break.
column8: 'Mittagspause' joins 'Mittag' and 'Pause'. You say 'Mittagspause machen' or 'in der Mittagspause'.
'Links' and 'rechts' never take an ending: they are invariable adverbs used for street directions.

column7: The post office is on the right.
column8: 'Nach rechts' indicates movement toward the right, while 'rechts' alone indicates a static position.
'Geradeaus' is a compound of 'gerade' (straight) and 'aus', now a single invariable adverb.

column6: Das Café ist an der Ecke.
column7: The café is on the corner.
column8: 'An der Ecke' uses the dative because it describes a fixed position, not movement toward the corner.

column6: An der Kreuzung biegen Sie ab.
column8: 'Abbiegen' is separable: 'biegen Sie ab' in the polite form, with the prefix detached at the end.

column6: Warte, bis die Ampel grün wird.
column7: Wait until the light turns green.
column8: 'Ampel' comes from the Latin 'ampulla' (small vessel): the historical name for the early oil lamps used as signals.

column7: Pedestrians have right of way here.
column8: German pedestrian zones ('Fußgängerzone') in old towns are often very large and closed to cars all day.
'Verkehr' also means 'contact/intercourse' in other contexts, as in 'Geschlechtsverkehr' (sexual intercourse).

column7: We're stuck in a traffic jam.
column8: German highways ('Autobahn') are famous for having no speed limit on many stretches, but also for long traffic jams.

column7: We couldn't find a parking space.
column8: In German city centers, parking is often paid and regulated by a mandatory parking-disc time limit.

column7: I don't have my ticket with me.
column8: On German public transport, ticket checks are often random, but fines for riding without one are very steep.

column6: Der Zug fährt von Gleis drei ab.
column7: The train departs from platform three.
column8: At German stations the platform can change at the last minute — it's always worth checking the boards.
'Fahrplan' is the timetable of trains and buses. For school it is 'Stundenplan', for work shifts 'Dienstplan'.
In Germany, tickets bought online often cost less than those bought directly on board.

column7: Tomorrow we're going on a trip.
column8: 'Einen Ausflug machen' is the standard structure for talking about trips — there's no simple verb 'ausflügen'.

column7: We often play cards in the evening.
column8: The activity is said in the plural: 'Karten spielen'. Singular 'Karte' is a single card, a ticket or a map.

column6: Die Kinder spielen mit dem Ball.
column7: The children are playing with the ball.
column8: 'Mit dem Ball spielen' uses the dative after 'mit', one of the most frequent dative prepositions of all.

column6: Fußball ist in Deutschland sehr beliebt.
column7: Football is very popular in Germany.
column8: The German Bundesliga is among the most-watched football leagues in the world, with some of the highest stadium attendance.

column7: We're going to the swimming pool.
column8: Many German towns run public municipal pools (an open-air 'Freibad' in summer) at very affordable prices.
'Sport treiben' is more formal than 'Sport machen', but both forms are correct and common.
'Joggen' is a direct loanword from English, now fully integrated into regular German conjugation.

column6: Ich gehe dreimal die Woche ins Fitnessstudio.
column7: I go to the gym three times a week.
column8: 'Dreimal die Woche' uses the temporal accusative, common for expressing frequency without a preposition.
'Handtuch' is a compound: 'Hand' (hand) + 'Tuch' (cloth), even though today it's used for the whole body.
'Riechen nach' takes the dative: 'nach Lavendel', used to describe a specific scent.
'Zahnbürste' is a compound: 'Zahn' (tooth) + 'Bürste' (brush), literally a 'brush for teeth'.
Singular 'Haar' can mean either a single hair or, colloquially, hair as a whole.
A well-groomed beard has come back into fashion in Germany over the last decade, especially among younger people.
'Brille' is singular in German for a single pair of glasses, while English uses the plural 'glasses'.
'Ganz Ohr sein' ('to be all ear') means listening very attentively, just like the English idiom 'all ears'.
'Die Nase voll haben' ('to have a full nose') means being fed up with something, just like English 'to be fed up'.
'Aufmachen' is separable: 'mach auf' in the casual imperative, with the prefix detached at the end.
The plural 'Zähne' takes an umlaut, like many short masculine nouns for body parts.

column6: Er hat sich das Bein gebrochen.
column8: 'Sich das Bein brechen' uses the reflexive dative 'sich' plus the accusative 'das Bein': the affected body part is the direct object.
'Arm' also means 'poor' as an adjective: two identically spelled words of completely different origin.

column6: Ich habe mir in den Finger geschnitten.
column8: 'Sich in den Finger schneiden' describes an accidental injury with the reflexive dative and the accusative of the affected part.
'Bauchschmerzen' (stomach ache) is a very common compound word parents use with small children.
'Hinter dem Rücken' ('behind the back') means doing something 'behind someone's back', just as in English.

column6: Er trägt die Tasche auf der Schulter.
column7: He carries the bag on his shoulder.
column8: 'Auf der Schulter' uses the dative because it describes a position, not movement toward the shoulder.
'Genießen' always takes a direct accusative object with no preposition: 'den Sonnenschein genießen'.

column7: The sky is full of clouds.
column8: 'Auf Wolke sieben schweben' ('to float on cloud seven') is the German equivalent of the English 'to be on cloud nine'.

column6: Heute Abend gibt es ein Gewitter.
column7: Tonight there will be a thunderstorm.
column8: 'Es gibt' plus the accusative is the standard structure for announcing weather events or the existence of something.
Sylt, in the North Sea, is one of the most exclusive beach destinations, beloved by well-off Germans.

column6: Wir liegen den ganzen Tag am Strand.
column7: We're lying on the beach all day.
column8: 'Am Strand' uses the dative because it describes where you are, a position, not movement.
'Sand ins Getriebe streuen' ('to sprinkle sand into the gears') means to sabotage or hinder a process.
'Welle' is also used figuratively: 'eine Welle der Solidarität' means 'a wave of solidarity'.

column6: Wir fahren mit dem Boot auf den See.
column7: We're going out on the lake by boat.
column8: 'Boot' and 'Schiff' aren't perfect synonyms: 'Boot' is small, while 'Schiff' means a large vessel.
'Angeln gehen' is a fixed expression: the noun 'Angeln' comes directly from the infinitive verb used as a noun.
Camping is a very popular summer activity in Germany, with organized campsites even by the big lakes.

column6: Wir machen am Abend ein Feuer.
column7: In the evening we make a fire.
column8: 'Ein Feuer machen' is the fixed structure for 'lighting a bonfire', different from 'anzünden' used for matches or candles.
'Rucksack' is a compound: 'Rücken' (back) + 'Sack' (sack), literally a 'back sack'.
'Landkarte' distinguishes the geographic map from the generic term 'Karte', which can also mean ticket or credit card.

column6: Der Weg zum Bahnhof ist kurz.
column7: The way to the station is short.
column8: 'Weg' means both a physical path and, figuratively, a 'way, means', as in 'to find a way, no matter what'.

column6: Wir fahren in die falsche Richtung.
column7: We're going in the wrong direction.
column8: 'In die Richtung' uses the accusative because it describes movement directed toward a specific direction.

column6: Wir kaufen einen Reiseführer für Berlin.
column7: We're buying a guidebook for Berlin.
column8: 'Reiseführer' means both the book and the person who guides tourists — two meanings in the same word.

column6: Der Kölner Dom ist eine berühmte Sehenswürdigkeit.
column7: Cologne Cathedral is a famous landmark.
column8: 'Sehenswürdigkeit' combines 'sehen' (to see) and 'würdig' (worthy): literally 'that which is worth seeing'.

column6: Kannst du bitte ein Foto machen?
column7: Can you please take a photo?
column8: 'Ein Foto machen' is the standard form; the verb 'fotografieren' exists but is slightly more formal.

column6: Ich kaufe ein Andenken für zu Hause.
column7: I'm buying a souvenir to take home.
column8: 'Andenken' comes from 'an etwas denken' (to think of something): an object that brings a place or person to mind.

column6: Wir überqueren die Grenze nach Österreich.
column7: We're crossing the border into Austria.
column8: Germany borders nine countries, the highest number of neighbors of any European state.

column7: She would like to visit abroad.
column8: 'Besuchen' always takes a direct accusative object with no preposition, like the English 'to visit'.

column6: Ich möchte eine neue Sprache lernen.
column7: I'd like to learn a new language.
column8: 'Lernen' is used for learning in general, while 'studieren' is reserved for formal university study.
'Wörterbuch' is a compound: 'Wörter' (words, plural of 'Wort') + 'Buch' (book), literally a 'book of words'.
'Üben' is regular and underlies 'Übung' (exercise), one of the most recurring words in learning materials.

column6: Es ist normal, Fehler zu machen.
column8: 'Fehler machen' is the standard structure; the infinitive with 'zu' follows precise rules after impersonal expressions like 'es ist normal'.

column6: Ich hoffe, die Prüfung zu bestehen.
column7: I hope to pass the exam.
column8: 'Bestehen' isn't separable: it belongs to the group of verbs with the always-inseparable prefix 'be-'.
